blocks: Stereo — width of Tilt and Spray
Dry/Wet — affects the Delay section only
Tilt — delays high frequencies more (positive) or low frequencies more (negative)
Spray — scatters delay times across frequencies at random
Mask — limits Tilt and Spray to highs (positive) or lows (negative)
Resolution, at the top right of the spectrogram, trades accuracy for latency. Lower it while recording to reduce latency.
Frz > Dly / Dly > Frz — order of the two sections
Dry/Wet — overall mix; 100% on a return track

Spectrum analyzes frequencies in real time and draws level (dB, vertical) against frequency or pitch (horizontal). Peaks stay on the graph until the song restarts. It measures only and never changes the sound.
Block — samples per measurement; more is more accurate and uses more CPU
Refresh — how often it analyzes; faster is more accurate and uses more CPU
Avg — how many blocks are averaged per update. 1 shows every block, good for finding short peaks; higher values give a smoother view closer to how we hear.
Graph — a smooth line or discrete frequency bins
Max — shows the accumulated maximum; click the display to reset it
Scale X — linear, logarithmic or semitone. Log and semitone are the same scale with Hz or note names along the top; linear helps when studying the highs.
Hovering shows level, frequency and note name at the pointer.
Range/Auto — Range lets you scroll (drag vertically) and zoom (drag horizontally) on the level legend, or set limits with the Range sliders; Auto scales to the input and disables those.
The title bar button, or double-clicking the display, moves the display into Live's main window.

Tuner shows the pitch of a monophonic input and how far it is from the nearest semitone. Its large display, modeled on guitar tuners, is readable on stage and suits tuning external instruments and synths.
It measures only and never changes the sound. It works best on a clean, single-note signal; chords, noise or very rich harmonics can confuse it.
Two buttons at the lower left switch between Classic View (like an analog tuner) and Histogram View (pitch over time). Green means in tune, red out of tune.
The pitch is a colored ball on a curve, with the nearest note name in the middle; arrows beside the name show whether to tune up or down.
Target Mode — a circle marks the target; the ball sits right of it when sharp and left when flat.
Strobe Mode — the curve becomes a rotating band of lights, turning right when sharp and left when flat, faster the further off.
Hertz/Cents — shows the frequency in Hz or the distance from the target in cents (also in Histogram View)
Pitch is drawn over time. Note names run down the right side; gray bars mark the exact center of each note, with sharp notes above and flat notes below.
Drag vertically to scroll and horizontally to zoom. Auto keeps the incoming pitch centered.
Right-click the display to choose note names: Sharps (C , Flats (D♭), or Sharps and Flats (C .
Reference — the tuning reference, 440 Hz by default (standard concert pitch), adjustable from 410 to 480 Hz.
Utility handles common signal tasks, often alongside other devices.
Phase — one switch per channel to invert left or right
Channel Mode — use only Left or only Right (on both outputs), for stereo files with different material on each side

Width — stereo width; 0% mono, above 100% wider. Mid/Side Mode in its context menu swaps it for a Mid/Side control: toward 100M sums to mono, toward 100S leaves only the side signal (left and right 180° apart). Width and Mid/Side are disabled when Channel Mode is Left or Right.
Mono — sums the input to mono
Bass Mono — makes the lows mono below Bass Mono Frequency (50–500 Hz), so they hold up on mono playback; Bass Mono Audition plays only those lows for tuning the frequency
Gain — −∞ to +35 dB. Handy for automating fades while leaving the track's Volume for mixing. Arrow keys step 1 dB from −18 to +35 dB and speed up below −18 dB.
Mute — silences the input at Utility's position. Since a track's own mute is at the end of the chain, Utility before a delay or reverb can cut its input and let the tail continue.
DC — removes DC offset and inaudibly low frequencies; matters only when nonlinear devices such as compressors or waveshapers follow
Related question: Ableton/Track/Q/How can I turn a mono signal into stereo in a channel?
Vinyl Distortion imitates the distortions of vinyl playback, which come from the geometry of needle and groove, and adds crackle.

Tracing Model — even harmonic distortion. Drive or vertical drag in its X-Y display sets the amount; horizontal drag or the Freq field sets its frequency ("color"); Option-drag (Mac) / Alt-drag (Windows) vertically sets Q.
Pinch Effect — odd harmonics, typically 180° out of phase for a wider stereo image; same controls, different sound.
Drive (global) — overall distortion from both sections
Soft imitates a dub plate; Hard a standard record.
Stereo/mono switch — whether the Pinch distortion is stereo (more realistic) or mono
Crackle — noise with Density and Volume
Vocoder is not in the Intro and Lite editions.

A vocoder imposes the level contour of one signal, the modulator (usually speech or drums), onto the frequencies of another, the carrier (usually a rich synth such as strings or a pad). The classic result is a talking synth or robot voice.
Both signals pass through banks of band-pass filters; the level in each modulator band sets the level of the matching carrier band.
Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:
Noise — internal noise; its X-Y display sets downsampling (horizontal, left lowers the sample rate) and density (vertical, down thins it)
Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:
External — any internal routing point; the usual choice for robot voices
Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:
Modulator — the modulator carries itself, a resynthesized version shaped by Vocoder's controls
Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:

Pitch Tracking — a monophonic oscillator that follows the modulator's pitch, limited by High and Low. Saw or three pulse waves, with Pitch for coarse tuning. It holds each detected pitch until it finds a new one, so changing its settings or resetting it (for instance by grouping the track) can change the sound unexpectedly. Best on single melodic lines or voice; unpredictable but interesting on chords and drums.
Put Vocoder on the modulator's track. Carrier options:
Enhance — normalizes the carrier's spectrum and dynamics for a brighter sound, useful with external carriers
Unvoiced — level of an extra noise source for pitchless sounds like "f" and "s"; Sens. sets detection (100% always on, 0% off); Fast/Slow how quickly it switches
The center display shows each band's level; click in it to lower bands.
Bands — number of filters; more is more accurate and uses more CPU
Range — frequency span of the filters; narrow it if the sound gets too piercing or boomy
BW — filter bandwidth; 100% is most accurate, other values can be interesting
Precise/Retro — equal gain and width for every band, or narrower, louder bands toward the top
Gate — bands below the threshold are silent
Depth — how much of the modulator's envelope reaches the carrier; 0% none, 100% classic vocoding, 200% only the loudest peaks
Attack and Release — response speed; very fast keeps transients but can distort
Channel switches — Mono (both mono), Stereo (mono modulator, stereo carrier), L/R (both stereo)
Formant — shifts the carrier's filter bank; small changes on a voice can change its apparent gender
Dry/Wet — balance of processed and dry signal
Setups for the most common uses.
1. Put Vocoder on the vocal track — a recorded clip, or a live mic chosen as the track input.
2. Put a synth such as Ableton/Live/UG/31 Instrument Reference/01 Analog on another track, played from a clip or live.
3. Set Carrier to External and pick the synth track in Audio From (Post FX in the lower chooser works best).
4. For live input, arm both tracks.
5. Play the synth while speaking: the speech rhythm comes through with the synth's tone. Solo the voice track to hear only the vocoded sound.
Bright, harmonically rich patches, such as saw-based ones, make the words clearer; Unvoiced and Enhance add more clarity.
Carrier Modulator, Depth 100%, Enhance on — then turn Formant to change the source's character, and try the filter bank controls too.
A reference entry for each built-in MIDI effect, such as Arpeggiator, Chord and Scale.
Arpeggiator turns a held chord or single note into a rhythmic pattern.
Style sets the order of notes in the pattern, and the display draws it. Previous and Next Style Pattern buttons in the display step through the styles.
Most styles are the usual ones: Up, Down, Converge, Diverge.
Style sets the order of notes in the pattern, and the display draws it. Previous and Next Style Pattern buttons in the display step through the styles.
Play Order plays notes in the order they were pressed.
Style sets the order of notes in the pattern, and the display draws it. Previous and Next Style Pattern buttons in the display step through the styles.
Chord Trigger repeats all held notes together as a block chord.

Style sets the order of notes in the pattern, and the display draws it. Previous and Next Style Pattern buttons in the display step through the styles.
Random Other — random, but no note repeats until every held note has played
Style sets the order of notes in the pattern, and the display draws it. Previous and Next Style Pattern buttons in the display step through the styles.
Random Once — one random pattern, repeated until the held notes change
Style sets the order of notes in the pattern, and the display draws it. Previous and Next Style Pattern buttons in the display step through the styles.
Rate sets the speed, in milliseconds or in tempo-synced divisions depending on the Sync/Free toggle.

Distance and Steps transpose the pattern on each repeat. Distance is the interval in semitones or scale degrees; Steps is how many transposed repeats follow. With Distance +12 st and Steps 2, a pattern starting on C3 plays at C3, then C4, then C5. Negative Distance goes down.
Root and Scale keep the transposition inside a scale. Use Current Scale in the title bar takes the clip's scale instead and disables those two choosers.
Gate sets note length as a percentage of Rate. Over 100% the notes overlap for a legato sound.
Hold keeps the pattern going after the keys are released, until a new key is pressed. Holding keys and adding more builds up the pattern; playing a held note again removes it.
Pattern Offset rotates the start of the pattern by a number of steps. At 1 the second note plays first and the first note plays last.
Groove adds swing from the groove library; the Global Groove Amount in the Groove Pool or Control Bar sets how strong it is.
Beat — every bar or beat set by Interval
An LED next to the Retrigger controls flashes on each restart.
Repeats sets how many times the pattern plays; the default is ∞. Values of 1 or 2 suggest a strummed guitar, and combining Repeats with Retrigger gives patterns with rests between them.

The Velocity toggle shows the velocity controls. Decay is the time to reach the Target velocity; a long Decay with Target 0 fades the pattern out. With Retrigger on, the velocity ramp restarts with the pattern.
CC Control sends MIDI CC messages to hardware. It has three fixed knobs, one custom button, and twelve custom dials.
Mod Wheel — modulation amount on the receiving device
Pitch Bend — bends down with negative values, up with positive
Custom A is a button that sends on/off or minimum/maximum. It defaults to the sustain pedal (CC 64) and can be set to any other CC with its CC Type chooser.
Custom B–M are dials that can be renamed and set to any CC. Names and assignments show on Push and are saved with presets. Automate them in lanes or turn the dials live.
two toggles switch between controls 1–8 and 9–16
Send sends every current CC value at once
Learn assigns a custom control from incoming MIDI, which also shows which CC a hardware controller sends
If the clip already has automation for a CC that CC Control also sends, the two streams are merged.
Chord adds up to six pitches to each incoming note.

Shift 1–6 each set one added pitch, up to ±36 semitones from the incoming note. Shift 1 at +4 st and Shift 2 at +7 st make a major chord on the played note. Order does not matter. An LED next to each Shift knob flashes when its note plays.
Two Shift controls cannot hold the same pitch; a duplicate is switched off.

Learn in the title bar sets the Shifts from a played chord: the first held key is the root and is not stored, and each further held key fills the next Shift. Hold more keys to add pitches, then turn Learn off.
With the Velocity or Chance toggle on, a slider under each Shift adjusts that note:
Velocity — relative to the incoming note, 1% to 200%; 100% matches it
With the Velocity or Chance toggle on, a slider under each Shift adjusts that note:
Chance — probability, 0% to 100%, that the added note plays
With the Velocity or Chance toggle on, a slider under each Shift adjusts that note:

Strum spreads the chord's notes over up to 400 ms. Positive values play the original note first, then Shift 1 to 6; negative values reverse that. Play Duplicate Notes When Strumming in the title bar's context menu allows repeated notes.
Tension — positive values start the strum slowly and speed up; negative values start fast and slow down
Strum spreads the chord's notes over up to 400 ms. Positive values play the original note first, then Shift 1 to 6; negative values reverse that. Play Duplicate
Crescendo — a rising (positive) or falling (negative) velocity ramp across the strum
Strum spreads the chord's notes over up to 400 ms. Positive values play the original note first, then Shift 1 to 6; negative values reverse that. Play Duplicate
Use Current Scale in the title bar changes Shift units from semitones to scale degrees.
Send Per Note Events to Generated Notes, in the title bar's context menu, passes MPE data to the added notes. With scale awareness on, per-note pitch bends follow the clip's scale.
Note Length changes the length of incoming notes, and can trigger notes from Note Off messages instead of Note On.
Trigger Source chooses Note On or Note Off.
With Note On, Length sets the base length and Gate scales it: 100% is the full Length, 200% doubles it, 50% halves it. The Time Mode toggles switch Length between milliseconds and synced divisions.
With Note Off, each note starts when the key is released, so it is delayed by its own held length. Gate and Length then apply. Three more controls appear:
Release Velocity — the mix of Note On and Note Off velocity used for the output note; leave at 0% if the keyboard sends no release velocity
With Note Off, each note starts when the key is released, so it is delayed by its own held length. Gate and Length then apply. Three more controls appear:
Decay Time — how long the velocity takes to fall to zero from the Note On; the value reached at Note Off becomes the output velocity
With Note Off, each note starts when the key is released, so it is delayed by its own held length. Gate and Length then apply. Three more controls appear:
Key Scale — positive values make notes below C3 longer and notes above C3 shorter; negative values reverse it
With Note Off, each note starts when the key is released, so it is delayed by its own held length. Gate and Length then apply. Three more controls appear:
with Note On, each note plays until the next Note On
with Note Off, a note triggers when all keys (or the sustain pedal) are released and a new Note Off arrives
in both cases Gate and Length are disabled; with Note Off, Release Velocity, Decay Time and Key Scale are disabled too
Pitch transposes incoming notes by up to ±128 semitones, or ±30 scale degrees with Use Current Scale on in the title bar.
Step Up and Step Down change Pitch by the Step Width (1–48 semitones, or 1–30 scale degrees). All of these can be key- or MIDI-mapped for changes during a performance.
Lowest and Range set the band of notes that pass. Mode decides what happens to notes outside it:
Block — they are dropped, and an LED next to Range flashes
Lowest and Range set the band of notes that pass. Mode decides what happens to notes outside it:
Fold — they are transposed into the range
Lowest and Range set the band of notes that pass. Mode decides what happens to notes outside it:
Limit — notes below are raised to the lowest note and notes above are lowered to the highest
Lowest and Range set the band of notes that pass. Mode decides what happens to notes outside it:
Random changes the pitch of incoming notes at random.
Chance is how likely each note is to be changed, like a dry/wet for randomness.

Choices (1–24) and Interval multiply to give the spread of possible pitches above, below or around the played note. With Chance 50%, Choices 1 and Interval 12, repeated C3s play C3 or C4. With Choices 12 and Interval 1, they play C3 or any note from C to C4. (Both examples use Random mode and Add.)

Alt — steps through the possible pitches in a fixed cycle. Chance 100% always moves to the next pitch; 0% always plays the incoming note. With Choices 12 and Interval 1, repeated C3s climb a semitone at a time to C4 and start over; with Choices 2 and Interval 2, they alternate C3 and D3 — useful for up-bow/down-bow or left/right hand samples.
LEDs beside Chance flash +, 0 or - for a higher, unchanged or lower note.
Use Current Scale in the title bar keeps random pitches in the clip's scale. Alt mode with a scale works like a simple, unpredictable step sequencer.
Scale remaps each incoming note to an outgoing note through a matrix, so every C can become a D, for example.

The Note Matrix is a 13 × 13 grid: columns are incoming notes in an octave, rows are outgoing notes. Black squares match the keyboard's black keys. Highlighted squares show the mapping, starting from the root in the bottom left.
Base sets the root and Scale Name the scale. Use Current Scale in the title bar takes both from the clip and disables those choosers.
Choosing User in Scale Name allows a custom mapping: drag highlighted squares to move them or click to delete them. A removed note is never output.
Transpose shifts notes by up to ±36 semitones; +7 st moves a C major melody to G major.
Fold, with User selected, folds any note mapped more than six semitones away back toward the original: a C3 mapped to A3 plays A2 instead.
Lowest and Range limit which notes are remapped (and transposed); notes outside pass unchanged. Lowest C2 with Range +36 affects only C2 to B4.
Velocity remaps incoming velocities (1–127) into a chosen output range.

The Velocity Curve grid maps the input range (Lowest and Range, X axis) onto the output range (Out Low and Out Hi, Y axis). Out Low 80 with Out Hi 127 makes even soft playing come out loud. Lowest and Out Low at 0 with Range and Out Hi at 127 leaves velocities nearly unchanged.
Operation applies the mapping to Note On velocity, Note Off (release) velocity, or both.
Mode handles velocities outside the input range:
Clip — clamps them into the range
Mode handles velocities outside the input range:
Gate — removes those notes; an LED under the grid flashes
Mode handles velocities outside the input range:
Fixed — every note gets the Out Hi velocity
Mode handles velocities outside the input range:
Random moves each velocity up or down by up to the set amount, inside the output range. A gray band around the curve shows the random spread.
Drive pushes the curve toward one end: positive values make most notes loud, negative values soft.
Compand spreads velocities toward the extremes (positive) or squeezes them toward the middle (negative).
A reference entry for each built-in instrument, such as Analog, Drift, Operator, Sampler, Simpler and Wavetable.
Analog is a virtual analog synth made with Applied Acoustics Systems. It doesn't copy one vintage synth; it combines features of several.
It uses physical modeling: equations for analog circuits are solved in real time, with no samples or wavetables.
Two oscillators and a noise generator feed two multi-mode filters, each followed by an amplifier. The filters can run in series or in parallel.
Two LFOs modulate oscillators, filters and amps, and each filter and amp has its own envelope.
The interface is a central display surrounded by the shell. The shell holds each section's main controls; the display shows the selected section's visualizations and extra controls.
A Global section holds volume, vibrato, polyphony and similar settings, and an MPE section maps pressure, slide and per-note pitch bend.
Modeled oscillators, so no aliasing. Each has an on switch (Osc 1, Osc 2) and a level slider.
F1/F2 — balance between Filter 1 and Filter 2; centered sends equally.
Shape — sine, sawtooth, rectangular or white noise. Rectangular enables Pulse Width (100% is a square with odd harmonics only; low values sound thin), which an LFO can modulate.
Octave, Semi, Detune — tuning; Detune moves in cents, up to 300 cents either way.

Pitch Mod — LFO amount, and Key: how far pitch follows the keyboard. 100% is equal temperament, 0% ignores note pitch. C3 always plays the same frequency, so oscillators with different Key values move further out of tune with each other the farther you play from C3.
Pitch Env — Initial pitch and the Time to glide to the final pitch.

Sub/Sync — Sub adds an oscillator an octave down (square for saw or rectangle, sine for sine, off for noise) at a set Level. Sync restarts the waveform from a hidden oscillator whose rate rises with Ratio; 0% has no effect. Mapping Ratio to a mod wheel is a suggested use.
White noise through its own -6 dB/octave low-pass filter, with an on switch and level.
Color — the low-pass frequency; higher is brighter.
Noise has shell controls only, so the display doesn't change.
Two multi-mode filters with independent settings, flexible routing, saturation and modulation.
Fil 1 / Fil 2 — on switches; the chooser beside each picks 2nd- or 4th-order low-pass, band-pass, notch, high-pass or formant.
Freq and Reso — cutoff and resonance. With a formant filter, Reso moves between vowel sounds. Filter 1's Freq:
To F2 (Filter 1) — how much of Filter 1's output feeds Filter 2.
Follow (Filter 2) — Filter 2's cutoff tracks Filter 1, including its modulation; Filter 2's Freq then sets the offset.
Freq Mod and Res Mod — modulation of cutoff and resonance by LFO, note pitch and filter envelope; negative values lower them.
Drive — saturation after the filter: Off, three symmetrical Sym modes, or asymmetrical Asym modes; higher numbers distort more.
After each filter an amplifier sets level and pan, with its own envelope.
Amp 1 / Amp 2 — on switches; Level and Pan knobs.
Pan Mod and Level Mod — modulation by LFO, note pitch and amp envelope. With note pitch on Level, middle C stays the same and positive values make higher notes louder.
Besides the oscillator pitch envelopes, each filter and amp has an ADSR envelope, all four with the same controls in the display, plus velocity and looping.
Attack, with Att < Vel to shorten it at higher velocities; Decay; Sustain (fully left removes sustain, fully right removes decay); Release.
Env < Vel — velocity scales the whole envelope.
S.Time — lets the sustain level fall while the key is held; lower is faster.
Legato — a note played while another is held continues that note's envelope.
Free — skips sustain and goes straight from decay to release, so notes have equal length; suits percussion.
AD-R — attack and decay repeat until release.
ADR-R — attack, decay and release repeat while held.
ADS-R — no looping, but attack and release play once more on key release, which can mimic audible dampers.
With Free on, AD-R and ADR-R act as if the key is always held.
Two independent LFOs that modulate oscillators, filters and amps.
LFO 1 / LFO 2 switches, Rate in Hz or tempo-synced divisions.
Wave — sine, triangle, rectangle, stepped random noise or smoothed noise. Width shapes triangle (toward up or down saw) and rectangle (pulse width); 50% gives a pure triangle or square.
Delay — time before the LFO starts; Attack — time to full depth.
Retrig — restart at the same phase on each note; Offset shifts the phase.
